title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM SAUL'S SPEAR
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM SAUL'S SPEAR
Some weapons never leave the hand.
Not because they are needed.
Not because they are useful.
But because the person holding them has become convinced that everyone around them is a threat.
I did not learn that lesson from a battlefield.
I learned it from a spear.
A single spear held by a king whose heart had drifted far from God.
Most believers know Saul as Israel's first king. Fewer understand the terrifying tragedy of what happened inside him.
Saul was not born a villain.
He was chosen.
Anointed.
Empowered.
Honored.
The Spirit of God came upon him.
He stood among prophets.
He experienced victories most people only dream about.
Yet when we meet Saul later in the biblical narrative, we find a man sitting with a spear constantly in his hand.
The spear became more than a weapon.
It became a symbol.
A mirror.
A revelation of what happens when insecurity sits on the throne of the human heart.
Scripture paints the scene with chilling repetition.
"And Saul had his spear in his hand."
The phrase appears again and again throughout his story.
The Hebrew word for spear is חֲנִית (chanith).
It was designed for war.
But Saul eventually used it against people who were never his enemies.
David.
Jonathan.
Even those closest to him.
The spear revealed something deeper than anger.
It exposed fear.
Fear almost always disguises itself as control.
The day David killed Goliath, everything changed.
Women began singing.
"Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands."
The words sounded harmless to everyone else.
To Saul, they sounded like a funeral bell.
Scripture says Saul became angry and suspicious.
Not because David had harmed him.
David had only helped him.
Not because David had betrayed him.
David was fiercely loyal.
Not because God had abandoned Saul that day.
The deeper problem was already growing inside him.
Jealousy.
Comparison.
Pride.
The hidden sins that rarely announce themselves until they have already poisoned the soul.
The Hebrew text says Saul "eyed David" from that day forward.
The phrase carries the idea of watching with hostility.
Looking through suspicion.
Interpreting everything through insecurity.
Suddenly every success David achieved felt like a personal attack.
Every victory became evidence of competition.
Every blessing became a threat.
And that is the danger of a heart disconnected from God.
When identity is no longer anchored in God, other people's success begins to feel like your failure.
You stop celebrating grace.
You start measuring worth.
You stop seeing brothers.
You start seeing rivals.
The spear always follows shortly afterward.
Maybe your spear is not made of wood and iron.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is gossip.
Maybe it is criticism.
Maybe it is resentment.
Maybe it is the endless need to prove yourself.
Maybe it is the inability to rejoice when God blesses someone else.
The weapon changes.
The heart condition remains the same.
Saul threw his spear at David while David played worship music.
Pause and think about that.
David was not attacking him.
David was serving him.
David was trying to soothe his troubled spirit.
Yet Saul responded with violence.
That is what happens when wounds go unhealed.
Eventually even kindness feels threatening.
Even love feels dangerous.
Even help feels offensive.
Many people are destroying relationships because they are throwing spears at people who are trying to help them heal.
But the story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Saul eventually throws a spear at his own son Jonathan.
Why?
Because Jonathan loved David.
The very people Saul should have cherished became targets of his rage.
Sin never stays contained.
The spear you throw at one person eventually threatens everyone around you.
Bitterness never remains isolated.
Jealousy never remains private.
Pride never remains personal.
Everything eventually spills over.
This is why Scripture takes the condition of the heart so seriously.
Jesus later taught the same truth.
The Greek word καρδία (kardia), meaning heart, refers not merely to emotions but to the center of a person's will, desires, thoughts, and spiritual life.
Jesus said in Matthew 15:19:
"For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander."
The problem is never merely external behavior.
The spear in the hand always begins as something growing in the heart.
Yet Saul's story is not only about a spear.
It is also about grace.
Because hidden within the darkness stands David.
David had opportunities to kill Saul.
More than once.
The cave.
The camp.
The vulnerable moments when revenge would have been easy.
No one would have blamed him.
Many would have applauded him.
Yet David refused.
Why?
Because David understood something Saul never learned.
God's purposes never need sinful shortcuts.
David trusted God's timing.
Saul grasped for control.
David surrendered.
Saul clung tighter.
One man carried a spear.
The other carried trust.
Only one walked away with peace.
The lesson becomes even more powerful when viewed through the Gospel.
David points us toward someone greater.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Like David, Jesus was innocent.
Like David, Jesus was rejected.
Like David, Jesus was hunted despite doing good.
But unlike David, Jesus did not merely dodge the spear.
He absorbed the wound.
Isaiah prophesied:
"But He was pierced for our transgressions."
The Hebrew word translated "pierced" is מְחֹלָל (mecholal), carrying the idea of being wounded, pierced through, or fatally injured because of another's guilt.
The spear that ultimately matters is not Saul's.
It is the spear that pierced Christ's side.
In John's Gospel, after Jesus died upon the cross, a soldier thrust a spear into Him.
Blood and water flowed out.
The King without sin received the wound sinners deserved.
The innocent was pierced so the guilty could be forgiven.
This is where the entire story turns from scandal to grace.
Saul teaches us what happens when we refuse surrender.
Jesus shows us what happens when we embrace it.
Saul clung to his throne and lost everything.
Jesus surrendered His life and redeemed everything.
Saul's spear brought fear.
Christ's wounds bring salvation.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated grace, means unearned favor, undeserved kindness, and divine generosity given to those who cannot earn it.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we dropped the spear.
Not that we fixed ourselves.
Not that we suddenly became worthy.
But that Christ stepped into our place while we were still sinners.
Every one of us has held Saul's spear in some form.
Every one of us has battled jealousy, pride, anger, fear, insecurity, comparison, or bitterness.
Every one of us has wounded others while protecting our own fragile kingdom.
Yet Jesus still comes.
Still calls.
Still forgives.
Still restores.
Still rewrites stories.
Maybe that is why Saul's spear continues to speak across thousands of years.
Because we recognize ourselves in it.
And because we recognize our hope in Christ.
The question is not whether you have ever held the spear.
The question is whether you are willing to lay it down.
What spear am I still carrying?
What relationship has my pride wounded?
What insecurity has stolen my peace?
What jealousy have I justified?
What bitterness have I protected?
Bring it to Jesus.
Lay it at the foot of the cross.
The same Savior who forgave Peter, restored Thomas, welcomed the thief, and redeemed countless broken sinners is still extending grace today.
And if this message challenged your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What spear is God asking you to surrender?
Be honest.
Someone else may find courage through your testimony.
The spear in Saul's hand exposed a broken king, but the wounds in Christ's hands revealed a perfect Savior.
